questions.stem: The LARGEST GLAND in the human body is:
questions.explanation: LIVER — largest gland + largest internal organ in the human body. Weight: ~1.5 kg in adults. Located in the upper right abdomen, under the diaphragm. Functions: (1) Produces BILE (stored in gallbladder, emulsifies fats in duodenum); (2) Metabolism of carbs (gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis), proteins (amino acid deamination, urea cycle), lipids; (3) Detoxification of drugs + alcohol; (4) Storage of glycogen, Vitamins A/D/B12, Iron, Copper; (5) Plasma protein synthesis (albumin, clotting factors); (6) Destroys old RBCs. Diseases: Hepatitis, cirrhosis, fatty liver, liver cancer. The PANCREAS (~80g) is the second-largest gland — has DUAL function: exocrine (digestive enzymes into duodenum — trypsin, lipase, amylase) + endocrine (insulin + glucagon into blood via Islets of Langerhans).

questions.stem: Digestion of STARCH begins in which part of the digestive tract, via which enzyme?
questions.explanation: STARCH DIGESTION: begins in the MOUTH via SALIVARY AMYLASE (PTYALIN), produced by SALIVARY GLANDS (parotid, submandibular, sublingual). Optimum pH 6.5-7 (neutral). Hydrolyses starch → maltose + dextrins. Chewing + saliva form the BOLUS. In the stomach (pH 1.5-3.5), salivary amylase is INACTIVATED (denatured by acid). Protein digestion starts in the STOMACH via PEPSIN (from pepsinogen, activated by HCl). Final digestion in SMALL INTESTINE: PANCREATIC AMYLASE (completes starch → maltose), PANCREATIC LIPASE (fats → fatty acids + glycerol), PANCREATIC PROTEASES (trypsin, chymotrypsin). Brush-border enzymes: maltase, sucrase, lactase (LACTOSE INTOLERANCE = lactase deficiency), peptidases. ABSORPTION occurs in SMALL INTESTINE (VILLI + microvilli). WATER + electrolytes absorbed in LARGE INTESTINE.

questions.stem: The approximate length of the small intestine in an adult human is:
questions.explanation: SMALL INTESTINE length: ~6 metres (20 feet) in an adult — but in a LIVING person it's shorter (~3-4m) due to muscle tone; cadaver measurements give 6m after relaxation. DIVIDED into 3 parts: (1) DUODENUM (~25 cm, 'C'-shaped, receives bile + pancreatic juice, site where most chemical digestion happens); (2) JEJUNUM (~2.5m, main absorption); (3) ILEUM (~3.5m, absorbs B12 + bile salts; ileocecal valve at end). VILLI + microvilli increase the surface area to ~250 m² (size of a tennis court!). LARGE INTESTINE ~1.5m. Parts: CECUM (with appendix — vestigial in humans), ASCENDING COLON, TRANSVERSE COLON, DESCENDING COLON, SIGMOID COLON, RECTUM, ANUS. Total GI tract: ~9 metres from mouth to anus. Stomach capacity: ~1-1.5 L (can stretch to 4L). Transit time: mouth to stomach ~seconds; stomach emptying 2-4 hours; small intestine 3-6 hours; large intestine 12-40+ hours; total ~24-72 hours.

questions.stem: BILE is produced by the LIVER and stored/concentrated in the GALLBLADDER. Its primary function in digestion is:

options.option_text: EMULSIFYING fats (breaking large fat droplets into tiny ones) to aid lipase action

questions.explanation: BILE is a green-yellow alkaline fluid (pH ~8) secreted by the LIVER (~0.5 L/day), stored + concentrated ~10× in the GALLBLADDER, released into duodenum via COMMON BILE DUCT when fatty food arrives (triggered by CCK hormone from duodenum). Bile composition: BILE SALTS (sodium glycocholate + taurocholate — derived from cholesterol — the active agent), BILIRUBIN (from RBC breakdown — causes yellow colour; excess → jaundice), CHOLESTEROL, phospholipids. FUNCTION: EMULSIFICATION of fats — bile salts act as DETERGENTS, breaking large fat globules into tiny micelles → massively increases surface area for PANCREATIC LIPASE. Bile is ESSENTIAL for digestion/absorption of fats + fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). GALLSTONES: crystallisation of cholesterol/bilirubin. Bilirubin retention → JAUNDICE (yellowing of skin + sclera).

questions.stem: Which enzyme in the stomach breaks down PROTEINS into smaller peptides, active in acidic pH?
questions.explanation: PEPSIN — the main proteolytic enzyme of the stomach. Secreted as an INACTIVE PRECURSOR (zymogen) called PEPSINOGEN by chief cells of the gastric glands. Activated by HCl (secreted by parietal cells — 0.5% HCl, pH 1.5-3.5). Pepsin cleaves proteins into smaller peptides; optimum pH ~2. Cannot digest the stomach itself because the stomach lining has a thick MUCUS layer + bicarbonate. RENNIN (CHYMOSIN) — another stomach enzyme, especially in INFANTS — curdles milk (casein + calcium). In small intestine: TRYPSIN + CHYMOTRYPSIN (from pancreas, activated by intestinal enterokinase; active at alkaline pH due to bicarbonate). Ulcers: H. pylori bacteria + NSAIDs disrupt mucosal protection, letting acid erode the lining (Nobel 2005 to Marshall + Warren for proving bacterial cause). Treatment: PPIs (omeprazole), H2 blockers (ranitidine), antibiotics. from pepsinogen, activated by HCl.

questions.stem: VITAMIN B12 absorption occurs in which part of the digestive tract, and requires which factor?

options.option_text: Ileum (last part of small intestine); INTRINSIC FACTOR

questions.explanation: VITAMIN B12 (cobalamin) absorption: (1) Dietary B12 (from animal foods — no plant source) is released by pepsin + HCl in stomach; (2) Binds to INTRINSIC FACTOR (IF) — a glycoprotein secreted by PARIETAL CELLS of the stomach — forming B12-IF complex; (3) B12-IF complex travels to the TERMINAL ILEUM (last 60-100 cm of small intestine); (4) Specific receptors (cubilin) absorb it. Without IF, B12 can't be absorbed — leads to PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA (megaloblastic anemia + neurological damage). Causes: autoimmune destruction of parietal cells, gastric surgery, strict vegan diet (long-term). Treatment: B12 injections + oral supplements (diet alone may not suffice). Other absorption sites: DUODENUM — iron, calcium, magnesium, fat-soluble vitamins; JEJUNUM — most nutrients, sugars, amino acids; ILEUM — B12, bile salts. from stomach parietal cells.

questions.stem: PERISTALSIS — the wave-like muscle contractions that propel food through the digestive tract — is a function of which type of muscle?
questions.explanation: PERISTALSIS = wave-like coordinated contractions of SMOOTH (involuntary) MUSCLES in the walls of the digestive tract. The gut wall has two muscle layers: CIRCULAR (inner, squeezes) + LONGITUDINAL (outer, shortens) — together they push food forward. Controlled by the ENTERIC NERVOUS SYSTEM (ENS) — often called the 'SECOND BRAIN' — ~500 million neurons embedded in the gut wall (Meissner's + Auerbach's plexuses). ENS operates independently + interacts with the autonomic nervous system (parasympathetic stimulates digestion; sympathetic inhibits — 'rest and digest' vs 'fight or flight'). Exception: swallowing starts as VOLUNTARY (tongue, skeletal muscles in upper pharynx) → becomes INVOLUNTARY (smooth muscle of esophagus onwards). SEGMENTATION = mixing action, also smooth muscle. MASS MOVEMENTS in colon (triggered by gastro-colic reflex after meals).

questions.stem: An adult human has how many permanent teeth?
questions.explanation: Adults have 32 PERMANENT teeth. Children have 20 MILK (deciduous/baby) teeth. Formula (one side of upper or lower jaw, then ×4): ADULTS: 2 incisors + 1 canine + 2 premolars + 3 molars = 8 per quadrant × 4 = 32. CHILDREN: 2i + 1c + 0pm + 2m = 5 per quadrant × 4 = 20 (no premolars in milk set). 3rd molars = WISDOM TEETH, erupt 17-25 years (may be impacted — often surgically removed). Tooth structure: CROWN (enamel — hardest tissue in body, 96% mineral), NECK (gum line), ROOT (cementum, pulp with nerves/blood). Internal layers: enamel → dentin → pulp. Cavities (DENTAL CARIES) caused by Streptococcus mutans + poor hygiene. FLUORIDE hardens enamel. Tooth types by function: INCISORS (cutting), CANINES (tearing), PREMOLARS + MOLARS (grinding). Humans are OMNIVORES — dentition reflects mixed diet.

questions.stem: The APPENDIX — a small blind tube attached to the CECUM — is considered:

options.option_text: A VESTIGIAL organ with possible minor role as reservoir for beneficial gut bacteria

questions.explanation: APPENDIX (vermiform appendix) — 5-10 cm finger-like tube attached to the CECUM (first part of large intestine). In humans, considered VESTIGIAL — evolutionary remnant of a larger structure seen in herbivorous ancestors for cellulose digestion (surviving herbivores like rabbits have massive caecum + appendix). Recent hypothesis (Parker et al., 2007): in humans, it may act as a 'SAFE HOUSE' for beneficial gut bacteria — during diarrhoeal infections, appendix bacteria can 'reseed' the colon afterwards. APPENDICITIS — inflammation due to blockage (fecalith, swollen lymphoid tissue) → pain (initially central abdomen → migrates to RIGHT LOWER QUADRANT / McBurney's point), fever, nausea. If untreated, can rupture → PERITONITIS (life-threatening). Treatment: APPENDECTOMY (surgery — either open or laparoscopic). First successful appendectomy: Claudius Amyand, 1735 (London). Humans can live normally without appendix. Gut microbiome research now suggests more functional relevance than previously thought.

questions.stem: The 'HUNGER HORMONE' — stimulates appetite + food intake — is:
questions.explanation: Key hormones regulating hunger/satiety: GHRELIN — 'hunger hormone' — secreted by the stomach when empty, signals hypothalamus to induce hunger. Levels peak before meals, drop after eating. LEPTIN — 'satiety hormone' — secreted by ADIPOSE tissue (fat cells); long-term regulator of food intake + body weight. Levels rise with fat mass (tells brain 'you have enough fat stored'). Obesity often involves leptin RESISTANCE. CCK (CHOLECYSTOKININ) — from duodenum — triggers gallbladder contraction + bile release AND satiety signal. SECRETIN — from duodenum — stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate + bile. GASTRIN — from stomach G-cells — stimulates HCl secretion. GIP (Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide) — GLP-1 (Glucagon-Like Peptide-1) — from gut — stimulate insulin release; GLP-1 is the basis of modern anti-diabetic + weight-loss drugs (SEMAGLUTIDE / Ozempic, Wegovy; Tirzepatide / Mounjaro, Zepbound). INSULIN — lowers blood sugar. GLUCAGON — raises blood sugar (alpha cells). produced by stomach lining.
